title: Open vs. Closed AI: What The Data Actually Shows
content_html:
By: Frank Downing

The debate over open-weight versus closed-weight models reignites every few months when a major new model is released. The market sees a new model and rushes to conclude either that open-weight models are commoditizing intelligence or that frontier AI companies are approaching superintelligence and pulling away. Arguments often follow about what this means for companies across the AI industry, national security, and geopolitics. The stock market typically overreacts in one direction or the other. The DeepSeek-like fallout following Moonshot AI’s release of Kimi K3, followed by rumors of U.S. government regulatory action and last Friday’s open-source love letter led by Microsoft and widely endorsed across the U.S. AI complex - with Anthropic a notable exception - is a quintessential example.

All of this is the natural discourse you would expect around possibly the most transformational technology of our lifetimes, especially given its exponential rate of change. Too seldom, however, do these discussions leverage concrete data to understand what is actually happening on the ground. This article is an effort to do just that. No single metric paints the full picture, and there are plenty of ways to nitpick the analysis, but we believe taking data-driven approach is necessary to ground discussions in the age of AI.

Assessing Capability: Observations on the Pareto Frontier

Artificial Analysis publishes what is probably the field’s broadest and most widely cited set of AI model benchmarks. Its Intelligence Index leaderboard is the most commonly cited view and provides a useful starting point for understanding which models have the highest average intelligence across a curated suite of benchmarks that Artificial Analysis evolves over time. As shown below, nearly all of today’s most intelligent models, with the exceptions of Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2, are closed weight.

What this simple view lacks, however, is any notion of cost. Adding cost as a second dimension lets us trace the Pareto frontier: at each level of intelligence, which model delivers that capability at the lowest cost? As businesses worldwide grapple with rising AI spending, model efficiency is becoming increasingly important. For a well-defined task, a rational business would want the cheapest model capable of getting the job done. The chart below plots the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score for leading models against their average cost per task. Closed-weight models dominate the high-intelligence end of the frontier, while open-weight models dominate the low-cost end.

This pattern generally holds not only for the Intelligence Index but also for the individual benchmarks that comprise it. Across the nine constituent benchmarks and the index itself, there are 73 Pareto frontier appearances. Those appearances are split almost evenly: 36 come from closed-weight models and 37 from open-weight models. OpenAI is the most Pareto-dominant model provider today, thanks to its GPT-5.6 lineup, with 17 appearances. DeepSeek is second with 15 appearances. A single provider can hold multiple spots on the Pareto frontier at the same time. Because of the intelligence per dollar delivered by GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra, and Sol, OpenAI often earns two or three spots along a benchmark's frontier. This is less often the case for Anthropic, whose models are generally more expensive and therefore usually appear on the frontier only when they achieve the benchmark's highest score.

When we rank each Pareto frontier from highest to lowest intelligence and average each provider's highest-ranked model per benchmark, the pattern becomes clearer. Open-model providers tend to occupy the lower-cost portion of the frontier and therefore have a higher average max rank, while closed-model providers tend to dominate the higher-intelligence end and have a lower average max rank, as shown below:

Market Signals: Follow the Token Spend

Combing through benchmark results is only a starting point, of course. Real-world usage gives us a better sense of model adoption and, ultimately, investment outcomes. OpenRouter’s public rankings dashboard is a fruitful source of information. About 60 trillion tokens flow through OpenRouter each week, up 20x year over year from about 3 trillion in July 2025, as shown below.

To get a sense of scale, Alphabet recently disclosed that its Large Language Model (LLM) Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) serve 22 billion tokens per minute, or about 222 trillion per week. This puts OpenRouter at roughly 27% of Google’s LLM API token volume. It is not a majority of the market, but it is large enough to provide a meaningful signal, even if OpenRouter likely skews toward developer and enthusiast audiences.

For the top 20 models over the last 30 days, OpenRouter provides inference volume measured in tokens. The data show that 76% of those tokens were consumed by open models. When we factor in each model’s price, however, the picture reverses: about 80% of the roughly $65 million spent on OpenRouter over the last 30 days went to closed-weight model providers.

The insight is that, while there is clearly a market for open models, the lion’s share of the economics currently accrues to closed-weight providers.

To see how this might be trending, we can examine provider-level share of API requests over the last year. Importantly, the chart shows share of requests, not share of tokens. It should be directionally indicative of usage trends but is not directly comparable with the volume and spending metrics above.

Closed-weight models gained request share through the second half of last year, but open-weight models have been gaining share in 2026. The most recent full week was split roughly 50-50 between providers categorized as open and closed. It is important to note that OpenRouter provides weekly detail for only the top nine providers. The remaining field, grouped as “Other,” accounts for about 10% of requests per week.

What happens if request share continues to shift toward open models and spending follows? The clearest beneficiaries would be cloud and accelerator providers. If AI spending is not near its peak - and we do not believe it is - compute consumption should continue to grow. Regardless of who wins at the model layer, accelerators will still be needed to produce tokens, and model diversity broadens the customer pool for companies that own this infrastructure. This is especially true for Nvidia. Because most models are trained on Nvidia infrastructure and it has the largest installed base, support for Nvidia hardware comes out of the box for any meaningful new model. Given this positioning, it was not surprising to see Microsoft and Nvidia as the two standard-bearers behind the recently released letter supporting open source.

One would think open-model dominance would leave frontier labs that sell higher-end, higher-cost models worse off, especially in the API portion of their revenue. The counterweight is that OpenAI and Anthropic, the two quintessential frontier AI companies, each have thriving agentic application businesses that operate higher in the stack than model APIs. We believe these businesses could offer a more durable, higher-margin position. OpenAI and Anthropic can, in theory, capture any cost advantage created by lower-cost open models, and they have more compute than their competitors with which to serve models at scale.

Put differently, companies investing Research and Development (R&D) and compute to train open models and then giving away the weights must still build products that generate enough revenue to sustain that investment. We think those products will look much like what OpenAI and Anthropic are already building. Visit Moonshot AI’s Kimi website, and it looks a lot like ChatGPT or Claude.

Conclusion

As noted in the introduction, the debate over open-weight and closed-weight models is multifaceted. But investors are ultimately trying to answer a simpler question: Where will most of the economics of the AI opportunity accrue? One straightforward indicator that cuts through the noise is who is growing fastest. Thus far, the frontier AI labs have outgrown the rest of the field. Anthropic has increased run-rate revenue tenfold in each of the last two years and, based on its latest reporting, could be on track to do so again in 2026. Fireworks AI, an inference-focused cloud serving open models, recently surpassed $1 billion in run-rate revenue and is growing 5x year over year. The hyperscalers, meanwhile, are accelerating off a larger - but not dramatically larger - base. Alphabet leads at 82% year-over-year growth, with Google Cloud now operating at an annualized revenue run rate of approximately $100 billion, based on their latest earnings report. Zhipu AI and MiniMax, the two publicly traded Chinese open-source model companies, reported 2025 revenue growth of 134% and 159%, respectively, but together generated less than $200 million in revenue.

Of course, this growth, especially among the frontier labs, will eventually need to translate into profitability. If industry estimates of inference margins above 70% are directionally accurate, more of that profitability should flow through to the company level as inference accounts for a larger share of compute. We look forward to learning much more as these companies move toward the public markets.

In the meantime, the charts presented in this article can help track the adoption of open-weight and closed-weight models in production, grounding future discussions in observable data.
